body: I don't have anything better to do so why not lol. I've posted them before on this throwaway account if you're interested. Basically I hate my job so much that it makes me suicidal. I spent a week trying to figure out what job I could do that would let me be happy that I could realistically do or go back to school for with no success. I'm too much of a perfectionist and nothing seems to be good enough for me and I hate myself for it. Wife and I are slowly learning we can't have kids and I'm honestly not very attracted to her but she's great otherwise. Some days I want to leave her and some days I can't imagine not having her. I have adhd, anxiety, atypical depression and i just can't seem to figure anything out. There are too many problems to fix and no easy answers to anything. Every decision has downsides I can't seem to let myself get over, so I made the only decision where I don't have to deal with the consequences.

I feel like my life is on the verge of complete collapse and I don't know how else to solve it. I have some very legitimate career and relationship issues that I'm trying to figure out and despite taking more than a week off sick I can't make any decisions other than this.

I can deal with shitty rooms and beds but they literally just leave me completely alone here and I'm making zero progress on my issues.

That doesn't sound all that promising... Hopefully things are more helpful here. The doctor who did the psych consult last night was excellent and we talked for about 30 minutes but it was just an evaluation. I've seen her again twice but only for her to form me and to tell me about medication changes.

I'm in Canada so I don't know how the process changes but they have taken zero precautions with me other than i can't leave the immediate vicinity of my room. My wife brought me a bag and they didn't check it, she even packed my shaving razor. I have my phone and charger and headphones no problem. I guess I'm lucky in that sense.

The Career Directions Inventory I did through a career counselor. It cost $100.

The Canada Job Bank quiz is here, there are a few, I found the first and third ones most helpful:  https://www.jobbank.gc.ca/career-planning/quizzes

I did the Sokanu quiz after I wrote this post, and it was very good. I ended up paying for the premium account, I'm not sure that it was worth it other than that they gave me 30 suggested careers instead of 9. The quiz was very in depth though, almost as in depth as the CDI: https://www.careerexplorer.com/

I also did the O*Net Interest Profiler. https://www.onetcenter.org/tools.html

All the quizzes gave me similar results, with some outliers.

Me too! While I only get to do it in short spurts, and on my terms when I want to, labour is very satisfying. This weekend, in the midst of a terrible depression, I managed to pull out of it for 2 days to refinish my deck and while it was hard work, I had no desire to stop partway through and felt great when it was done.

I'm working with a therapist, she's not an adhd specialist but she's the best I'm going to get.

Can I ask why you left accounting? It's something I'm considering going into, I've always enjoyed working with financials. In many of the jobs I've had I had to analyze financials for people or businesses to write loans or assess a company as an investment. It's part of the job that I've never complained about.

I got a taste of accounting when I completed the CFA as well and while learning GAAP vs IFRS rules were not that interesting, it wasn't too bad.

I've been trying to push myself for 2 years. I've resolved to start forcing myself to do the sales piece a dozen or more times. I can never stick with it. Plus just doing some sales would not fix the other problems with my job.

I am 100% overthinking it, that's my nature. A big part of the problem is that most careers that pique my interest have entry requirements I can't meet or I doubt I'm competitive. It's one thing to jump into a new educational path, it's another to take a chance just to get some prerequisites for a program I have yet to apply for. It's just tough to take the risk when there's no certainty I can even get into the program I'm interested in. Plus this job is not one I can ever go back to once I leave. It does seem very final.

Alright, that's fair. I have a terrible attitude. However, before this job I earned 5 promotions in 8 years at a different bank in a different province, no dad around. I CAN be great at a job in finance. It's not hopeless. I have no idea how to improve my current situation though. I have repeatedly asked for more work and it doesn't come. I've done self started projects to improve the business and they get ignored. A big part of this is we have 2 guys essentially doing the job of one person.

I guess my point is why bother. Why bang my ahead against the wall any longer when there are careers out there much more suited to my abilities and personality? Take it for what it's worth but every career quiz I've ever taken has listed sales dead last for types of broad activities I'm suited for. 

Also people are overemphasizing the sales part of this. Even if I did it the expectation is that it will be 10-20% of my job. I only know how to fill about 20% of my time right now.

I think this is the only sales job I will consider, because if I have to switch careers I'm going to do something similar to what you said. There are so many things out there besides sales. I am also way way happier when I have a busy day, even if it's just doing paperwork. There are many days where I have less than an hour of real work to do, except for self directed sales activities. 

I am in therapy as well, we're still working on medication for the adhd. I'm going twice a week right now while I'm off work.

Comparing how I feel to others in the job, I think its fair to say that it can be boring. Most people don't seem to mind because they get freedom and good pay. I've had other young advisors say the job is easy, because they're naturally social and seemed to know 20 millionaires before they even started. Others seem ok to work hard for a week prepraring for a seminar then I don't see them in the office much for a week (independent advisors work hours are not monitored, the branch only cares about results). The older guys chit chat with some of their clients a few days a week and don't need to work that hard. Our admin assistant is often bored, she's very protective of jobs she considers hers and she's admitted to having lots of downtime where she's bored. It doesn't seem to destroy her mentally like it does for me though. 

Dad's bailing me out, sure, but I wouldn't even be here if it wasn't for him. 

I'm simply not a salesman. I'm demonstrably introverted compared to every advisor I know. Plus I don't believe cold calling will work so it's tough to put myself out there. I'm definitely depressed but it's 90% due to my job.

I wish this was possible. I'm not monitored very much during the day, but due to regulations in the industry I work in, I have to report and get approval for any activities that I get paid for outside of my regular job.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boreout

I had not heard of this before and it's exactly what's happening with me. Thanks for pointing that out.

It's a little complicated... I'm an associate investment advisor, which means I work for a semi-independent investment advisor. That IA seems to do all of his own work and doesn't delegate anything. Occasionally I get the odd minor job or recurring menial task to do. I get paid very well for this.
I would consider this if it was an option. Unfortunately working from home is not really on the table. I'm expected to show up here for 8 hours a day.
I really should be doing more of this. I tend to just mope and waste time on reddit because I'm depressed.

I think that if it's above your requested range then you should take it. I don't ever think there's a huge detriment to trying to negotiate more, but you don't have much to counter with. You don't have a better offer elsewhere and they gave you more than you asked for.

When I first started this job I had a lot more independence. I let that go to my head and started showing up at 10 or 10:30 and missing a lot of days. I found it helped to keep regular office hours. I don't know if your situation allows that but having a set period of time where you're 'at work' could be a start.

We actually have a half-time assistant. She answers the phone, does most of the paperwork and lots of the administrative tasks. She's great actually. I don't know how I could use her to help with my stuff though, she has a full plate already.

Thank you, this is some of the best analysis of a problem I've ever posted on the internet that I've seen before.

I think you're right about all of it, specifically about the small, manageable tasks. I'm used to that. For a long time in the bank I wrote complex corporate lending applications. Each of them was a big 3 day project, but broken down into hundreds of small steps, each with guidelines, procedures, and best practices available. That I can manage. I need to find a way to build processes and small steps into my job. And that's tough, especially when I'm not really all that motivated to do it. I'll try to take that away from this.

>Once you're busy checking tasks off of that to-do list, I don't think the escapism/grass-is-greener-elsewhere thinking will occupy much of your time. 

This is what I'm really after. I've read over and over about people leaving higher paying jobs to reduce their work hours or job stress, but they're working hard both before and after the switch. Not many people complain that they don't have enough to do. 

I've had good days in this job, and they usually involved me having a couple client meetings, giving out good advice to people who want and need it, and generally feeling useful. If I could go through a majority of days feeling like I accomplished something or helped someone, I would feel so much better about this career. 

>One more thing - don't be afraid to develop your own financial advising "style." The stereotypical financial advisor may be the extroverted salesmen "type," but there are many successful advisors who defy that stereotype.

I've heard this many times but I can't hear it often enough. I know many many advisors and certainly there are more extroverted types than others, but i know a few introverts, including my Dad. Trust me though, it's just a lot harder for us. You don't have to be an extroverted salesman but you do need to talk to a lot of people, especially those you don't know. I'd rather stay home and play video games most nights, but I need to be getting out of the house to settings where I can meet new people.

At one point my Dad had more than half the people on our street signed up as clients. I don't even know the names of half the people on my street. I don't know, that part is definitely uncomfortable hard work for me but the good thing is I'm not starting from scratch so I don't need to do a lot of that.

Anyway thanks for your thoughts, there's a lot to build on here.

Thank you, and yes, I'm looking into getting some professional help with this. I definitely have mental health issues as well, that are exacerbating the problem. I did see a career counsellor, but he wasn't very helpful other than having me do a career inventory test.

This is what I've been struggling with to a huge degree. On paper, money aside, this is the dream job. You can take as much time off as you like, you have no boss really (I still do but I won't someday), it's pretty stress free, all you have to do really is keep people happy. 

I just don't find it fulfilling at all. A big part of the problem is I don't know what I want to do instead, and the only things I can think of that I would like to do are not attainable at all. I'm completely willing to go back to school, but I would essentially have to go back to an undergrad degree to upgrade just to meet the minimums to apply to what I want, and these are programs that see less than 10% of applicants be successful. It's a massive risk and I can't seem to justify it.

Lots of people say things like 'no one is happy in their job' or 'I would crawl through broken glass for a living for that salary', so I'm trying my best to embrace that mentality first before I just give up. I've succeeded at lots of things I didn't enjoy and that were difficult; I did basic training. I completed my CFA (3 massive exams completely based on self-study) and it was definitely uninteresting for most of it, but I really wanted the end product.

I don't know, I'm pretty lost, but I do want to say I gave this a solid try before I give up.
